decision: Workers are pluggable across three engines chosen per worker: claude-cli (claude -p, default), codex-cli (codex exec --json), agent-sdk (@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY).
rationale: Operator requirement that all options be available; the CLI engines reuse the subscription login, the SDK engine gives in-process control where an API key is acceptable.
alternatives: Single engine (claude -p only) rejected by operator.

decision: The worker scheduler and runner run inside the Next.js web process, started from instrumentation.ts, with a Postgres advisory lock for single-leader execution.
rationale: The web plane already owns Postgres and (since #501) the Docker socket; no third process in any deployment mode.
alternatives: Dedicated daax-workers service (third process, new compose/CI wiring); terminal plane (no Postgres).

decision: Use croner for cron expression parsing and next-fire computation.
rationale: Zero dependencies, MIT, supports UTC evaluation.

decision: The Technical Project Manager worker defaults to propose autonomy: reads everything, writes nothing; merge/push/deploy/delete are denied at every autonomy level via tool deny-lists, not prompts.
rationale: Unattended scheduled and continuous runs must not change external state without an explicit operator opt-in per worker.
alternatives: act by default (unattended writes to Backlog/GitHub); observe (no proposals).

decision: Voice uses the browser Web Speech API for input (existing VoiceInput) and speechSynthesis for output; no server-side speech service.
rationale: No new service or cost; reuses the existing component.
alternatives: Server-side Whisper/TTS (new service, better accuracy, cost).

decision: The workers CLI ships in this repo as bun run workers, a thin client over the /api/workers REST API.
rationale: One API for UI, CLI and voice; ships with the feature.
alternatives: Add commands to the Go daax-cli (separate repo and release train).

decision: Worker write limits are enforced by the engines' own permission controls built from a per-run MCP tool listing; tools are read-only only by readOnlyHint or read-word naming, unknown tools are writes, and servers that cannot be listed are dropped.
rationale: Prompt-only restrictions are not enforcement; the backlog MCP server ships no annotations and uses noun_verb names, so both annotation and word-based classification are needed, and unclassifiable tools must fail closed.
alternatives: Prompt instructions only (unenforced); per-server all-or-nothing access (too coarse: blocks reads or allows writes); maintaining hand-written per-server tool lists (drifts).

decision: Claude CLI workers run with --setting-sources "" and --permission-mode dontAsk; codex workers run with an isolated per-run CODEX_HOME holding only a generated config and the operator's login.
rationale: Workers must not execute the operator's personal hooks or MCP servers; --bare was rejected because it disables OAuth/subscription login. Verified on claude 2.1.283/2.1.261 and codex 0.154.0/0.153.4.
alternatives: --bare (API key only); inheriting user settings (runs personal hooks and extra MCP servers inside unattended runs).

decision: The Workers module ships at beta maturity and read endpoints use requireAuth while mutations and run triggers use requireRole (workers:manage admin-only, workers:run admin+user).
rationale: alpha would hide the module at the default beta visibility; requireRole writes an audit row per call and the run view polls every 2s.
alternatives: alpha maturity (hidden by default); requireRole on reads (audit table flooded by polling).

decision: Worker reports render through a small in-repo markdown renderer that builds React elements and links only http(s) URLs, instead of adding a markdown dependency.
rationale: Reports use a narrow markdown subset; building elements (no HTML strings) makes report text unable to inject markup, and avoids a new dependency.
alternatives: react-markdown + remark-gfm (new dependencies); dangerouslySetInnerHTML with a sanitizer (injection risk surface).

decision: Workers get no shell at any autonomy level; git and GitHub state is collected by daax with fixed read-only execFile commands and given to the agent as project signals, and act-mode writes go only through MCP tools.
rationale: Codex review showed prefix rules cannot make a shell read-only (git diff --output=<file> writes; gh ... --body-file reads a local file and posts it).
alternatives: Allow-listed Bash prefixes (bypassable); OS sandboxing of the agent shell (not available uniformly across host macOS and the container image).

decision: Worker run history is redacted before storage, MCP credentials are confined to their own server's config, and daax/engine environment variables can never be passed through to MCP servers.
rationale: Codex review: tool output and errors were persisted verbatim and readable by any authenticated user; envPassthrough accepted DATABASE_URL; all servers' env was merged into the agent env.
alternatives: Trusting operator configuration (a single mistaken passthrough leaks the database credential to an LLM agent).

decision: Run lifecycle hardening: one deadline from claim, cancel requests persisted and applied by the leader, host runs in their own process group, labelled worker containers, orphan cleanup before interrupted runs are failed, leadership published only after recovery, deposed leaders abort their runs, stale completions ignored.
rationale: Codex review found paths where two executions of one worker could overlap or a cancelled run kept running.
alternatives: Per-run ownership tokens in the schema (stronger fencing, more complexity; the status-guarded finishRun plus abort-on-loss covers the single-operator deployment).

decision: MCP readOnlyHint annotations remain trusted for tool classification; the documented control for what a third-party MCP server can change is giving it read-only credentials.
rationale: Codex r2 noted annotations are self-declared. A server is arbitrary operator-chosen code: refusing its annotations would not stop it writing inside a 'read' tool, while it would block legitimate read tools. Credentials are the enforceable boundary.
alternatives: Per-worker hand-maintained tool allowlists (drift, operator burden); ignoring annotations (blocks legitimate reads without adding real protection).

decision: Host executor refs record pid and process start time; recovery signals a host process group only when both still match, and waits for verified termination (containers removed, groups gone) before interrupted runs are released.
rationale: A recycled pid could otherwise make recovery kill the operator's own claude/codex session; releasing a run before its predecessor stops could run a worker twice.
alternatives: Name-based process matching (kills unrelated sessions); no host recovery (orphans keep running after a crash).

decision: Crash recovery identifies host executions by a daax-run:<run id> marker in the agent's command line and releases a run only after its execution is verified stopped; ambiguous cases (recorded group alive, no marked process) stay locked until an operator force-releases them.
rationale: Codex r4 showed pid/start-time and group-liveness inference can match an unrelated group reused during downtime. macOS ps cannot read process environments, so the marker lives in argv. Keeping ambiguous runs locked fails safe (a stuck worker, never a killed unrelated process or a double execution).
alternatives: Environment-variable marker (unreadable on macOS); pid/start-time only (misses leader-exited groups); releasing ambiguous runs (possible double execution).

decision: Recovery identifies a host execution by a fresh random per-execution nonce stored only in its executor reference and placed on the engine command line, combined with a strict engine-executable check.
rationale: Codex r6/r7 showed that ps flattens argv, so text parsing of a guessable id (the run id) can match an operator's own commands (workers logs <id>, curl, rg, a prompt quoting the flag). A secret random nonce cannot occur in unrelated command lines by chance.
alternatives: Matching the run id (guessable, appears in logs/URLs); environment markers (unreadable on macOS); argv parsing heuristics alone (ambiguous after flattening).
